title: How the GC finds garbage
cards/0/body: In C# you create objects with new but never delete them by hand. The garbage collector (GC) does that: every so often it finds objects nobody needs anymore and frees their memory.
cards/1/body:
The GC starts from roots: local variables of running methods and static fields. From there it follows references. Everything it can reach is alive. The rest is garbage.

Think of a bunch of balloons: cut the string in your hand, and every balloon tied to it floats away.
cards/1/deep: CPU registers, GC handles (pinned objects, for example) and the finalization queue also count as roots. The JIT knows where a variable is last used: in a Release build an object can become garbage before the method ends. That's what GC.KeepAlive is for: it extends the lifetime up to a given line.
cards/2/task: Get rid of Log while keeping Order, Item and Price.
cards/3/q: order = null. What happens to Order → Item → Price?
cards/3/options/2: Nothing: their references to each other keep them alive
cards/3/explain: Item and Price are reachable only through Order. No path from a root means the whole chain is garbage.
cards/4/task: A and B reference each other. Clear the root and run a collection. Are they removed?
cards/5/q: Why doesn't the A ⇄ B cycle bother the collector?
cards/5/options/0: The GC looks for what is reachable from roots; it doesn't count references
cards/5/options/1: The GC breaks cycles on a timer
cards/5/options/2: It does bother it: that's a memory leak
cards/5/explain: Cycles are a problem where memory is freed by reference counting (like ARC in Swift). Tracing from roots simply never reaches them, so they get removed.
cards/6/body:
After freeing the garbage, the GC slides live objects closer together. That's compaction. New objects are then allocated back to back, very quickly.

Program threads are usually paused briefly during a collection.
cards/6/deep: Allocation in .NET is just bumping a pointer in the thread's "allocation context", so new is very cheap. What's expensive is surviving collections. There are Workstation and Server GC modes, background Gen 2 collection and GCSettings.LatencyMode.
cards/7/q: What counts as a GC root? Select all that apply.
cards/7/options/0: A local variable of a running method
cards/7/options/2: A field of an object nobody references
cards/7/options/3: Any object older than a minute
cards/7/explain: Roots are things that are definitely in use right now: thread stacks and static fields. A field of an unreachable object is not a root.
cards/8/q: When does a garbage collection run?
cards/8/options/0: When the runtime decides, usually when Gen 0 fills up
cards/8/options/1: As soon as an object becomes garbage
cards/8/explain: Garbage can sit around for a while. The GC kicks in once enough new memory has been allocated. More on that in the next lesson.
